what: GM Research's 'Digital Design' (later DAC-1) interactive graphics design system shown working at General Motors, 1959

sources.title: DAC-1
sources.quote: The system, known as Digital Design, was demonstrated and improved throughout 1959.

note: Rejected later candidates: DAC-1 full demo at IBM Kingston Dec 1962, Sketchpad (Sutherland, Jan 1963 report), DAC-1 public unveiling 1964; Hanratty's PRONTO (1957) is numerical-control programming, not interactive design by computer. The 1959 date rests on one Wikipedia statement and the early system's scope is unclear.

what: Production DAC-1 went live at GM in Warren, Michigan, used to design automobile parts (trunk lid modelled Nov 1963)

sources.title: DAC-1
sources.quote: The production DAC-1 system went live in Warren in April 1963.

note: Sketchpad (1963) was a thesis research system, not production. Earlier numerical-control tools (PRONTO 1957) are machining aids and were not counted. Not exhaustive for other countries (e.g. Citroen SPAC, Renault, 1960s).

what: Robot Scientist 'Adam' (Aberystwyth/Cambridge, Ross King) autonomously generated and tested hypotheses on yeast genes and found new knowledge

sources.title: Robot Scientist
sources.quote: Adam became the first machine in history to have discovered new scientific knowledge independently of its human creators.

note: Year 2009 (Science, 2 April 2009) is from memory/first pass: the pages I could reach (Wikipedia only) give no year. Earlier candidates: DENDRAL (1960s, Stanford; Wikipedia says it aimed to study hypothesis formation and discovery in science) and Meta-DENDRAL (mid-1970s, proposed new mass-spectrometry rules) are partial fits (analysis and rule induction but no experiments, human-directed) and I could not source dates. So earlier event may exist.

what: Test at Bedford, Massachusetts: radar data sent over telephone lines to a computer (Whirlwind), showing detection of a mock enemy aircraft; directed by C. Robert Wieser

sources.title: Semi-Automatic Ground Environment
sources.quote: data produced by a radar was transmitted through telephone lines to a computer for the first time, showing the detection of a mock enemy aircraft.

note: Earlier candidates: wartime radar/teleprinter links and Bell Labs relay computers remote-operated by teletype (1940 Complex Number Calculator demo, not checked here). Later: SAGE network 1958, SABRE 1960, CTSS 1961, ARPANET 1969. Chose 1951 test as first computer reached over lines from a distant sensor; not exhaustive.

what: SAGE New York sector became operational: computers linked by telephone/modem lines to radar sites and other centers in routine air defense

sources.title: Semi-Automatic Ground Environment
sources.quote: On "June 26, 1958,…the New York sector became operational"

note: Later: SABRE airline reservations 1960 (Wikipedia Computer network: 'In 1960, the commercial airline reservation system semi-automatic business research environment (SABRE) went online'), CTSS remote users. Pre-SAGE operational use (e.g. Cape Cod System tests from 1953, manual-era links) were tests, not service.

what: First ARPANET message UCLA to SRI (Wikidata inception of the Internet)
note: Only fits the network part of the definition (not worldwide, not for ordinary people). Considered: Minitel trial 15 July 1980 (national, terminals in homes), CompuServe/MicroNET consumer service 1979 (commercial online, not worldwide), WWW system working end of 1990. A stricter reading of the definition would put the demonstration around 1990-91.

what: The World (Brookline, MA) served its first customer, the first commercial Internet service provider offering the public direct access

sources.title: Internet service provider
sources.quote: Its first customer was served in November 1989.

note: Earlier home-terminal services (Minitel 1980-82 in France, CompuServe 1979) were not the Internet. Australian ISP also 1989.

what: Public use of the Internet and Web took off after NSFNET was decommissioned and traffic opened to commercial providers

sources.title: Internet
sources.quote: Since 1995, the Internet has tremendously impacted culture and commerce

note: Year is a judgement; the source supports 1995 as a turning point, not a user count. Adoption by ordinary households was later (2000s) in many countries.

what: MIT's CTSS MAILBOX let users of the same time-sharing computer leave messages for one another

sources.title: Email
sources.quote: Computer-based messaging between users of the same system became possible after the advent of time-sharing in the early 1960s, with a notable implementation by MIT's CTSS project in 1965.

note: First pass confirmed. Earlier: SAGE/AUTODIN style message switching (not user-to-user mail) not counted.

what: First ARPANET network mail sent (Ray Tomlinson, BBN), introducing user@host addressing

sources.title: Email
sources.quote: In 1971 the first ARPANET network mail was sent, introducing the now-familiar address syntax with the '@' symbol

note: Wikidata gives invention 1971 as well. Mass adoption not sourced: Wikipedia only says email is ubiquitous, no date.

what: Lockheed completed the earliest form of Dialog under Roger K. Summit, an online interactive retrieval system

sources.title: Dialog (online database)
sources.quote: The earliest form of the Dialog system was completed in 1966 in Lockheed under the direction of Roger K. Summit.

note: Earlier candidate: MEDLARS (NLM, 1964), a batch computer retrieval service, not interactive 'in seconds'; also pre-computer mechanical retrieval (Goldberg's Statistical Machine, 1931) rejected as not computerized.

what: MEDLINE, the online version of NLM's MEDLARS, became available for interactive searching from remote medical libraries

sources.title: MEDLINE
sources.quote: In late 1971, an online version called MEDLINE (MEDLARS Online) became available as a way to do online searching of MEDLARS from remote medical libraries.

note: Rejected earlier: MEDLARS 1964 (launched by NLM, 'first large-scale, computer-based, retrospective search service available to the general public') was a real service but batch-mode, so it does not meet 'in seconds'. Dialog commercial service started ~1972 (not sourced). If batch counts, practical use is 1964.

what: IBM Watson answered open-domain Jeopardy! clues in natural language and beat champions Rutter and Jennings (matches taped Jan 2011, broadcast Feb 2011)

sources.title: Watson (computer)
sources.quote: in 2011, the Watson computer system competed on Jeopardy! against champions Brad Rutter and Ken Jennings, winning the first-place prize of US$1 million.

note: Rejected earlier: BASEBALL (1961) and LUNAR (1971) answered questions only in narrow databases (Wikipedia: 'effective in their chosen domains'), so they do not match 'broad knowledge, arbitrary questions'; SHRDLU (blocks world) likewise. Web QA like Ask Jeeves (1997) matched questions to pages. Broad-domain systems may exist between 1990-2010 (e.g. START) which I could not source.

what: Apple's Siri introduced on the iPhone 4S, letting consumers ask questions in ordinary speech

sources.title: Virtual assistant
sources.quote: The first modern digital virtual assistant installed on a smartphone was Siri, which was introduced as a feature of the iPhone 4S on 4 October 2011.

note: Siri is a general assistant, not purely factual QA, and answers many questions via external services; fit is partial.

what: George Yevick and Adnan Wally invented an e-reader with a liquid-crystal display

sources.title: E-reader
sources.quote: The first e-reader was invented by George Yevick and Adnan Wally in 1972.

note: Source says invented and never commercialized; unclear whether a working unit was built. Dynabook (Kay, 1968-72) was a concept only.

what: Rocket eBook (NuvoMedia) went on sale in late 1998 as an early commercial handheld e-reader storing ten books; SoftBook and others appeared around 1998

sources.title: Rocket eBook
sources.quote: The Rocket eBook is an early commercial handheld e-reader that was produced by NuvoMedia in late 1998

note: Replaces the first-pass 2004 Sony Librie (first E Ink reader, not first reader). Sony Data Discman (1990) played CD-ROM books and is listed by Wikipedia among first commercial e-readers; not dated by a fetched source, so 1990 may be earlier. Mass adoption (Kindle, 2007; sold out in hours) left unsourced for a fetched page.

what: Nick Sheridon at Xerox PARC developed Gyricon, the first electronic paper (rotating two-color balls)

sources.title: Electronic paper
sources.quote: Electronic paper was first developed in the 1970s by Nick Sheridon at Xerox's Palo Alto Research Center.

note: Source says only 1970s; 1974 or 1975 per first pass. Earlier rewritable displays (liquid crystal, electrophoretic displays of the 1970s by others) not examined.

what: Sony Librie in Japan, first e-book reader with an E Ink electronic paper display

sources.title: Electronic paper
sources.quote: In 2004, Sony released the Librié in Japan, the first e-book reader with an electronic paper E Ink display.

note: Possibly earlier: Gyricon and E Ink signage and electronic shelf labels around 1999-2003 (no fetched source; NCR electronic shelf labels 1997 used other display tech). Librie is the first source-confirmed consumer product.

what: First practical optical holograms recording 3D objects made by Denisyuk (USSR) and by Leith and Upatnieks (Michigan), viewable from several angles

sources.title: Holography
sources.quote: the first practical optical holograms that recorded 3D objects to be made in 1962 by Yuri Denisyuk in the Soviet Union

note: Static holograms are a loose match for a 'display'. Other candidates: 1966 varifocal-mirror volumetric display (Volumetric display page), 1972 moving white-light hologram (Lloyd Cross), 1989 MIT electroholographic video display. Perspecta (2001) rejected as late. Gabor 1947-48 holography produced no 3D display.

what: MIT Spatial Imaging Group pioneered electroholography, an electronically driven moving 3D holographic display

sources.title: Holographic display
sources.quote: 1989 – MIT spatial imaging group pioneered electroholography

note: This is a lab system, so really a second demonstration; no routine practical use of holographic displays found. Treat as low.

what: MIT Whirlwind computer solved an equation and displayed the solution on an oscilloscope (third quarter of 1949)

sources.title: Whirlwind I
sources.quote: In the third quarter of 1949, the computer was advanced enough to solve an equation and display its solution on an oscilloscope

note: Earlier: Manchester Baby (June 1948) and EDSAC (1949) had CRTs showing memory contents (Williams-tube monitors) but for engineers, not as output display; not counted.

what: Whirlwind became operational in 1951, real-time output on CRT displays used in Cape Cod radar tracking

sources.title: Whirlwind I
sources.quote: Operational in 1951, it was among the first digital electronic computers that operated in real-time for output

note: Display-specific operational use date is approximate; SAGE-like display uses (1951 Bedford test) are the same era.

what: Bedford, MA test: radar data sent by phone line to a computer, displaying a mock enemy aircraft detection (Whirlwind)

sources.title: Semi-Automatic Ground Environment
sources.quote: data produced by a radar was transmitted through telephone lines to a computer for the first time, showing the detection of a mock enemy aircraft.

note: Other candidates: DATAR (Royal Canadian Navy/Ferranti, trial late 1953 on Lake Ontario, displays on plan-position indicators), Cape Cod System tests from Sept 1953, Royal Navy CDS (analog, 1940s). 1951 is earliest found.

what: SAGE New York sector became operational, direction-center consoles showing radar tracks from the computer

sources.title: Semi-Automatic Ground Environment
sources.quote: On "June 26, 1958,…the New York sector became operational"

note: First pass said 1958-07-01 at McGuire AFB; fetched page gives 26 June 1958 for New York sector. DATAR was not fielded; CDS-based Royal Navy ADA later.

what: E. A. Johnson (Royal Radar Establishment, Malvern) published a finger-driven capacitive touchscreen for air traffic control

sources.title: Touchscreen
sources.quote: He described his work on capacitive touchscreens in a short article published in 1965

note: Earlier: AT&T Harmon 1962 patent for a light-beam stylus touchscreen (patent only, not shown working). Data gloves: Sayre Glove 1977, later. Light pens (1950s) are pointing devices, not touch.

what: CERN transparent capacitive touchscreen (Beck and Stumpe) put into use for the SPS control system

sources.title: Touchscreen
sources.quote: Manufactured by CERN and later by industry partners, it was put to use in 1973.

note: Also PLATO IV optical touch terminals (patent filed 1972) used in education; and Johnson's was used in air traffic control, unverified.

what: Touchscreen phones were rapidly gaining popularity by 2009 after the 2007 LG Prada and iPhone

sources.title: Touchscreen
sources.quote: By 2009, touchscreen-enabled phones were rapidly gaining popularity

note: Date is a judgement (2007-2010). iPhone announced Jan 2007; first-pass 2007 date replaced by when popularity is stated.

what: David Shepard and Harvey Cook built the 'Gismo' reading machine after WWII; Shepard founded Intelligent Machines Research Corp in 1952 to commercialize it

sources.title: David H. Shepard
sources.quote: In 1952 he formed Intelligent Machines Research Corporation to commercialize the invention with William Lawless Jr. in Arlington, Virginia.

note: Date is a latest bound (Gismo built earlier, undated). Earlier: Tauschek and Goldberg 1929-31 optical-code readers, Goldberg 1915 patent, Optophone 1914 (read letters to the blind) are analogues that don't convert characters to data for computers.

what: US Post Office put the first high-speed optical character reader into operation for preliminary mail sorting

sources.title: Mail sorting
sources.quote: In 1965, the postal service put the first high-speed optical character reader into operation that could handle a preliminary sort automatically.

note: Earlier practical use likely: Shepard's Farrington B reader for credit-card slips ('first major industry use of OCR', undated) and 1950s commercial readers. Detroit detail not confirmed.

what: Creeper, an experimental self-replicating program by Bob Thomas (BBN), moved between PDP-10s over ARPANET; Reaper antivirus followed in 1972

sources.title: Computer virus
sources.quote: Creeper was an experimental self-replicating program written by Bob Thomas at BBN Technologies in 1971.

note: Earlier: von Neumann's 1949 theory of self-reproducing automata (theory only), MIT student phone and computer hacking 1959-63 (The Tech 1963, no actual break-in source), Equity Funding data fraud from 1964 (insider fraud). Later: Elk Cloner 1982, Brain 1986.

what: Morris worm spread across the Internet, disabling many machines

sources.title: Morris worm
sources.quote: The Morris worm or Internet worm of November 2, 1988, was a malicious self-replicating computer program that affected VAX computers

note: Earlier real-world attacks: Elk Cloner (1982, floppy virus in the wild), Brain (1986), Equity Funding records fraud from 1964 (insiders). Chose the first widely disruptive network attack; earlier smaller incidents likely exist.

concept_note: Moved earliest date from 1963 Sketchpad to GM Digital Design/DAC-1 (1959 demo, April 1963 production); no mass_adoption sourced.
Kept Adam 2009 (low: year not on reachable pages); DENDRAL/Meta-DENDRAL considered but undated by fetched sources and not clearly independent discovery; no practical use or mass adoption.
Moved demonstration back to 1951 radar-to-computer test, practical use to SAGE 1958; ARPANET 1969 not first; no mass adoption (Internet concept covers it).
Definition is composite; ARPANET 1969 as network demonstration (low), 1989 ISP as practical use, 1995 as mass adoption turning point (low); Web 1991 not used.
First pass confirmed (CTSS 1965, ARPANET 1971) with sources; mass adoption not sourced.
Demonstration Dialog 1966, practical use MEDLINE late 1971 (interactive); MEDLARS 1964 batch rejected for seconds requirement; no mass adoption sourced.
Kept Watson 2011 as first broad-domain; BASEBALL/LUNAR rejected as narrow; added Siri as low-confidence practical use; no mass adoption.
Practical use moved from 2004 Librie to 1998 Rocket eBook; added 1972 Yevick/Wally concept (low); mass adoption (Kindle 2007) unsourced so omitted.
Kept Gyricon 1970s and Librie 2004, both low; earlier signage/shelf-label e-paper possible but not sourced; no mass adoption.
Moved from 2001 Perspecta to 1962 holograms (low); electroholography 1989 as later lab step; no real practical use or mass adoption.
Moved from 1951 to 1949 Whirlwind oscilloscope display; practical use 1951 approx; no mass adoption sourced.
Moved demonstration to 1951 Bedford radar test (before SAGE); practical use SAGE New York sector 26 June 1958; DATAR 1953 noted.
Kept Johnson 1965; added CERN 1973 practical use and ~2009 phone popularity (low); gloves 1977 later.
Moved earlier to Shepard Gismo/IMRC 1952 (low); kept 1965 USPS as practical use (low); no mass adoption.
Creeper 1971 as demonstration and Morris 1988 as practical use (mapping loose); earlier insider fraud and phone hacking noted; no mass adoption.

_tools: WebSearch worked; WebFetch and page_text failed for all non-Wikipedia hosts (proxy 403 / host not allowed) except computerhistory.org; Wikipedia via page_text worked; chronam not used. All sources are Wikipedia/Wikidata so are reference-grade only; several dates lack contemporary sources.
